objectives: Define SNARK and trace Pinocchio → Groth16 → PLONK lineage with their trusted-setup trade-offs.
Distinguish arithmetization formats: R1CS, QAP, AIR, Plonkish, Halo2, ACIR.
Compare polynomial commitment schemes: KZG, FRI, IPA/Bulletproofs.

slides.title: SNARK = Succinct Non-interactive ARgument of Knowledge: Pinocchio → Groth16 → PLONK
slides.body:
A **SNARK** is a proof system with:

- **Succinct**: proof size + verification time are sub-linear (ideally polylog) in the size of the computation being verified.
- **Non-interactive**: a single message from prover to verifier (after one-time setup).
- **ARgument**: computationally sound (vs perfectly sound; trades infeasibility for efficiency).
- **of Knowledge**: prover must know a witness — extractor can recover it.

A **zk-SNARK** adds zero-knowledge: the proof leaks nothing about the witness.

**Lineage**:

**(1) Pinocchio (Parno, Howell, Raykova, Gentry 2013)** — first practical zk-SNARK. Built on QAPs (Gennaro-Gentry-Parno-Raykova 2013). Proof ~288 bytes, verification ~10 ms. Per-circuit trusted setup.

**(2) Groth16 (Jens Groth 2016)** — the most succinct SNARK to date. Proof = **3 elliptic-curve points** (~200 bytes); verification = 3 pairings. Per-circuit trusted setup (powers-of-tau + circuit-specific). Powered **Zcash Sapling (2018)**, Tornado Cash, Filecoin. Limitation: setup must redo for every circuit.

Use the visualization below to explore proof generation + verification for Groth16 with a 1024-constraint circuit.

**(3) Sonic (Maller-Bowe-Kohlweiss-Meiklejohn 2019)** — first **universal + updatable** trusted setup (one setup serves all circuits up to bounded size). Inspired PLONK + Marlin.

**(4) PLONK (Gabizon, Williamson, Ciobotaru 2019)** — *Permutations over Lagrange-bases for Oecumenical Non-interactive arguments of Knowledge*. Universal setup, KZG polynomial commitments, custom-gate-friendly arithmetization (Plonkish). The dominant modern SNARK. Variants: **TurboPLONK, UltraPLONK, plookup, HyperPlonk**.

**(5) Marlin (Chiesa-Hu-Maller-Mishra-Vesely 2020)** — universal SNARK with KZG commitments. Mary Maller + Pratyush Vesely are key authors.

**(6) Halo (Bowe-Grigg-Hopwood 2019)** + **Halo2 (Zcash 2020)** — IPA-based, **no trusted setup**, recursion via nested proofs. Powers Zcash Orchard + many Ethereum L2s.

**Trusted vs transparent setup**:

- **Per-circuit trusted setup**: Groth16. Must redo per circuit. Lowest proof + verification cost.
- **Universal trusted setup**: PLONK, Marlin. One setup serves all circuits ≤ size N.
- **Transparent setup (no toxic waste)**: STARKs, Halo2, Bulletproofs. Stronger trust model; larger proofs.

**Powers of Tau ceremonies**: thousands of participants each contribute randomness; security if ≥1 honest. Zcash, Filecoin, Ethereum KZG ceremonies have each had >100K participants.

slides.title: Arithmetization: R1CS, QAP, AIR, Plonkish, Halo2 circuits, ACIR
slides.body:
**Arithmetization** = encode a computation as a system of polynomial equations over a finite field. The prover proves they know a satisfying assignment.

**(1) R1CS — Rank-1 Constraint System**: a set of equations of the form (a · z)(b · z) = (c · z), where z is the witness vector + a, b, c are constant vectors. Each equation is **one multiplication** + arbitrary linear combinations. Foundation of Pinocchio, Groth16, Spartan. Compilers (circom, ZoKrates, snarkjs) emit R1CS from high-level code.

**(2) QAP — Quadratic Arithmetic Program**: turn R1CS into polynomial form. For m constraints, define polynomials A_i(X), B_i(X), C_i(X) interpolating a_i, b_i, c_i values at m points. R1CS satisfaction ⟺ polynomial divisibility: (Σ z_i A_i)(Σ z_i B_i) − (Σ z_i C_i) = h(X) · t(X), where t(X) vanishes on the constraint points. Used in Groth16.

**(3) AIR — Algebraic Intermediate Representation**: STARK arithmetization. Computation = sequence of state transitions; AIR specifies transition + boundary constraints as low-degree polynomials over an execution trace. Used in StarkWare's Cairo, RISC Zero, Boojum, Polygon zkEVM.

**(4) Plonkish**: PLONK's arithmetization. Witness arranged as a table (rows = gates, columns = wire values); constraints are polynomial identities on columns + permutation arguments link copies of the same wire. Supports **custom gates** + **lookups (plookup, halo2-lookup, lasso)** for efficient operations (range checks, XOR tables, elliptic-curve ops). Dominant modern format.

**(5) Halo2 circuits**: Zcash's Plonkish variant. Configurable advice/instance/selector columns, lookups, gate composition. Powers Zcash Orchard, Scroll, Taiko.

**(6) ACIR — Abstract Circuit IR**: Aztec's Noir language IR. Backend-agnostic — compile once, target Barretenberg (UltraPLONK), Halo2, or generic backends.

**Compilers + tooling**:
- **circom** (iden3): R1CS for Groth16/PLONK.
- **ZoKrates**: high-level → R1CS or Marlin.
- **Cairo** (StarkWare): for STARKs / AIR.
- **Noir** (Aztec): ACIR + multiple backends.
- **Leo, Halo2-DSL, snarkVM**: Aleo's privacy-preserving smart contracts.
- **Lurk, Plonky2/3** (Mir, Polygon): newer recursive provers.

**Witness encoding** — the gulf between high-level code + R1CS is significant; quadratic blowup in constraint count for many ops (hashes, ECC) is the bottleneck. Optimizations: lookup arguments, custom gates, MSM-friendly fields.

slides.title: Polynomial commitments: KZG, FRI, IPA, Bulletproofs
slides.body:
A **polynomial commitment scheme** lets a prover commit to a polynomial p(X), later open p(z) = y at chosen points z with a short proof. The foundation of every modern SNARK.

**(1) KZG (Kate-Zaverucha-Goldberg 2010)** — pairing-based. Setup: trusted ceremony produces ([1]₁, [τ]₁, [τ²]₁, ..., [τ^N]₁) for secret τ. Commitment to p(X) of degree ≤ N: C = [p(τ)]₁. Opening at z: witness π = [(p(X) − p(z))/(X − z)]₁. Verify via pairing equation e(C − [y]₁, g₂) = e(π, [τ − z]₂).

- **Pros**: **constant-size** commitment (1 group element) + opening (1 element). Verifier O(1).
- **Cons**: trusted setup, pairings (not post-quantum), bounded degree.
- **Used in**: PLONK, Marlin, Groth16 (with QAP), EIP-4844 'blob' transactions, Ethereum Verkle trees (planned).

**(2) FRI — Fast Reed-Solomon IOP of Proximity (Ben-Sasson-Bentov-Horesh-Riabzev 2018)** — hash-based. Tests that a function f is close to a low-degree polynomial via recursive folding: at each round, fold f(X) + f(-X) using a random challenge; ends in a single value. Verifier checks a logarithmic number of Merkle openings.

- **Pros**: **transparent setup** (no toxic waste), post-quantum (only hash + field assumptions), recursive-friendly.
- **Cons**: larger proofs (~100 KB), more verifier work (~log²).
- **Used in**: STARKs, RISC Zero, StarkWare, Plonky2/3 (Polygon), Boojum.

**(3) IPA — Inner Product Argument**: based on **Bulletproofs (Bünz et al. 2017)** — Pedersen commitments + recursive log-folding. Commit to vector v as C = Σ v_i G_i + r H. Prove inner product ⟨v, w⟩ = y by log-folding.

- **Pros**: transparent, no pairings, small commitments.
- **Cons**: linear verifier time (no succinctness in verification).
- **Used in**: Halo2 (Zcash), Bulletproofs (Monero range proofs), Spartan.

**(4) Bulletproofs (Bünz, Bootle, Boneh, Poelstra, Maxwell 2017)**: a complete proof system on top of IPA. Specialized for range proofs (Monero confidential transactions).

**Comparison**:

| Scheme | Setup | Proof | Verif | PQ? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KZG | Trusted | O(1) | O(1) | No |
| FRI | Transparent | O(log²) | O(log²) | Yes |
| IPA | Transparent | O(log) | O(n) | No |

**Modern hybrid**: many systems compose schemes — e.g., Halo2 uses IPA for transparency; PLONK uses KZG for succinctness; Plonky2 uses FRI for post-quantum + recursion-friendliness.

**Folding schemes** (Nova 2021, ProtoStar 2023) extend polynomial commitments for **incrementally verifiable computation** — accumulate proofs over many steps without growing proof size. The frontier of recursive proving.

question.question: Arithmetize y = x³ + x + 5 into R1CS
question.goal: Express the cubic computation as a Rank-1 Constraint System ((a · z)(b · z) = (c · z)).

steps.prompt: Decompose y = x³ + x + 5 into elementary multiplications.
steps.reveal: Decompose into: (1) x₂ = x · x; (2) x₃ = x₂ · x; (3) y = x₃ + x + 5. The final step is linear, not a multiplication.

acceptedAnswers: z = (1, x, x2, x3, y) or similar

steps.reveal: Witness z = (1, x, x₂, x₃, y). Index 0 = constant 1; remaining = wires. Public input: y. Private witness: x, x₂, x₃.

steps.prompt: Write the R1CS constraint for x₂ = x · x.
hints: a · z = x; b · z = x; c · z = x₂.

steps.prompt: Write the constraint for the linear y = x₃ + x + 5.
steps.reveal: Linear constraint via (a)(1) = c: a = (5, 1, 0, 1, 0) (= 5 + x + x₃), b = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0) (= 1), c = (0, 0, 0, 0, 1) (= y). Each linear constraint costs 1 R1CS row. Total: 3 constraints for this circuit. Modern compilers (circom) automate this.

question.finalResult: y = x³ + x + 5 arithmetizes to 3 R1CS rows. QAP transforms this into polynomial-divisibility check over a finite field; Groth16 then proves this in ~200 bytes. For large circuits (e.g., hash function), R1CS row count drives prover cost — main bottleneck of modern SNARKs.

question.question: What is the key trade-off between KZG and FRI polynomial commitments?
options: KZG is faster, FRI is slower — no other differences.

KZG has constant-size proofs + O(1) verification but requires a trusted setup and is not post-quantum (uses pairings); FRI has transparent setup + is post-quantum but produces larger O(log²) proofs and slower verification.
question.explanation: **KZG (Kate-Zaverucha-Goldberg 2010)**: constant-size commitments + 1-element opening proofs verified via 1 pairing. **Requires trusted setup** (toxic waste τ) + relies on pairing-friendly curves → NOT post-quantum. **FRI (Ben-Sasson-Bentov-Horesh-Riabzev 2018)**: transparent (only hashes), post-quantum, but produces O(log²) proofs (~100 KB) + O(log²) verification. Trade-off: KZG for short proofs in trusted-setup OK environments (PLONK, Groth16, Ethereum 4844 blobs); FRI for transparency + post-quantum (STARKs, RISC Zero, Plonky2).

slides.workedSolution: KZG: trusted setup, pairings (not PQ), O(1) proof + verif. FRI: transparent, hash-based (PQ), O(log²) proof + verif. Choice depends on application: KZG for short proofs (PLONK, Groth16); FRI for transparency + PQ (STARKs).

question.question: Choose a SNARK system for a use case
question.prompt: You're designing (a) a one-shot proof system for a fixed Merkle-tree-inclusion circuit deployed on Ethereum, (b) a universal rollup that must support many evolving circuits, (c) a post-quantum-safe identity system. Recommend Groth16, PLONK, or STARK for each + justify.

question.question: Groth16 proof size: how many group elements?
question.hint: Two G₁ points + one G₂ point.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the three-layer architecture of a modern SNARK: arithmetization (R1CS/AIR/Plonkish) → polynomial encoding → polynomial commitment. Why this layering, and how does it affect proof size, prover cost, and setup requirements?
question.rubric: Mentions: arithmetization encodes computation as polynomial equations (R1CS, QAP, AIR, Plonkish). Polynomial encoding (QAP, AIR) turns constraints into polynomial-divisibility checks. Polynomial commitment scheme (KZG, FRI, IPA) lets prover commit to + open polynomials succinctly. Layering enables mix-and-match: PLONK = Plonkish + KZG; STARK = AIR + FRI; Halo2 = Plonkish + IPA. Affects proof size (KZG O(1), FRI O(log²), IPA O(log)), verifier cost, and setup (KZG trusted; FRI/IPA transparent). Pinocchio 2013 → Groth16 2016 → PLONK 2019 → Halo2/Plonky2 today. Parno, Howell, Raykova, Gentry, Groth, Maller, Bowe, Kate-Zaverucha-Goldberg, Ben-Sasson, Riabzev all key contributors.
